rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a people remain indifferent, God gives them respite until truth leaves no legitimate excuse, then destroys them; the Messenger must keep warning during that period.
rows.anchor: if his people remain indifferent to it, then after giving them respite for a certain period of time, the Almighty necessarily destroys them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger must continue communicating and warning until God tells him the task is complete; he must not decide by his own assessment to leave.
rows.anchor: consign their fate to Him and migrate from that land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah was rebuked after deciding to leave on his own; 68:48 likewise tells Muhammad to wait patiently rather than repeat that haste.
rows.anchor: be not like the companion of the fish, (68:48)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse protects Muhammad from haste by making the decision to end his warning mission God's, not his own.
rows.anchor: this decision was not to be taken by him; it was to be taken by God

rows.speaker: Exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes read the verse as forbidding a favor given for greater return; Islahi says this is possible but contextually wrong as the verse's correct meaning.
rows.anchor: was not to do a favour to someone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verse conveys the same instruction of patience and perseverance, continuing the coherence of the warning passage.
rows.anchor: here in this sūrah too, the next verse conveys precisely the same message to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the preposition li, ṣabr means waiting with patience and perseverance; the Prophet must persist and await his Lord's decision.
rows.anchor: it means to wait with patience and perseverance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This continues the preceding instruction: do not stop the effort as sufficient, since patient persistence completes the communication of truth and supports the Prophet's success.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) should not discontinue his endeavour at some stage regarding it to be sufficient

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trumpet heralds a severe Judgment Day for Quraysh, who deny its likelihood, expect worldly privilege to continue, or rely on their deities' intercession.
rows.anchor: will be very severe for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negative phrasing is subtle sarcasm at disbelievers who dismiss the Day; it warns that the opportunity to prepare exists only now, and the unprepared cannot be rescued.
rows.anchor: the day will not at all be an easy one to contend with; it will be very tough

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affluent leaders of Makkah and Ṭāʾif mistook wealth for proof that they were God's favorites and expected still more; Muhammad should leave their fate to God.
rows.anchor: These verses admonish the megalomaniac leaders of Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording resembles 73:11, where Muhammad is also told to leave the comfortable rejecters to God for a little respite.
rows.anchor: I have explained it there

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being created alone means entering life without wealth, status, companions, or confidants; these are God's favors and should inspire gratitude, not entitlement to more in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: when man comes into this world, he is without wealth and status and without comrades and confidants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage describes a general wealthy, high-status mentality, not Walīd ibn Mughīrah alone, though it applies to him too.
rows.anchor: there is no reason for restricting the verse to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Early scholars' reports that a verse was revealed about a person can mean that person is one application, not the occasion of revelation; the passage diagnoses a common arrogant mentality.
rows.anchor: they do not necessarily imply

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word used for the person can refer to singular or plural antecedents, fitting the passage's general application.
rows.anchor: used here which is used for both singular and plural entities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bestowed wealth was spread across different locations and ventures, like modern capitalists' international accounts and investments.
rows.anchor: in every country and investments in companies found all over the world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God also gave him sons who supported his many business ventures; in tribal society family numbers and defense were central to status and survival.
rows.anchor: supporters in every place and front

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of the sons as present points to their being capable and alert enough to stand by their father when needed.
rows.anchor: the sons too had to be so capable and alert that they could stand by the side of their father whenever any need arose

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and sons paved the way to social respect, dignity, leadership, and influence.
rows.anchor: society was paved for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such favors should have made him grateful and obedient, but he became arrogant and claimed he would receive even more in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The obligation of divine favours bestowed on him was that he be a grateful and obedient person to his Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic denial rebuts the arrogant man's claim: his favors were unearned gifts testing whether he would be grateful or rebellious, and he failed the test.
rows.anchor: they had earned them through their own planning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Our revelations” means the Qur'an generally, especially its warnings of worldly and next-world punishment and its teaching that God alone governs both realms.
rows.anchor: those who warn them of worldly punishment and the one they will face in the next world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahaq means putting someone through hardship.
rows.anchor: means “to put someone through hardship”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaʿūd means a peak or steep slope that is very difficult to climb.
rows.anchor: a peak or a steep slope which is very difficult to climb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The steep ascent punishes ingratitude: after receiving favors, the arrogant worshiped their wealth and desires and forgot its giver.
rows.anchor: they started to cherish and worship these favours

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Virtue brings immediate hardship but deferred reward, while vice offers immediate pleasure and deferred punishment; perseverance is needed to resist desire.
rows.anchor: the pleasures of vice are immediate and its pangs have been deferred to the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To illustrate perseverance on the hard path, the author cites Jesus's teaching that the narrow way leads to life while the easy broad way leads to destruction.
rows.anchor: While pointing to this aspect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 90:10–20 the steep path means freeing a slave or feeding an orphan or indigent person in famine, along with faith, patience, and compassion; those who surmount this virtue path succeed, while others face Hell's ascent.
rows.anchor: the steep path of virtue in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He delays his reaction after hearing the Qur'an so onlookers will think their leader is considering it seriously.
rows.anchor: took some time to ponder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After pondering, he carefully weighed his opinion so that his words would take root with listeners and appear credible.
rows.anchor: he thoroughly weighed the opinion that came to his mind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated curse before his verdict condemns both the hideous opinion and the foolish, self-important way he imagines a pebble to be a pearl.
rows.anchor: a pebble is a pearl

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an depicts his arrogance: he assesses listeners' moods, frowns to signal a hopeless judgment, then turns away muttering.
rows.anchor: he lifted his face assessing the faces of the people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He calls the Qur'an magic and human speech; Quraysh used the magic label as propaganda after they could no longer deny its eloquence and force.
rows.anchor: they embarked upon a propaganda campaign against it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By calling it inherited magic, opponents claimed its spellbinding effect was merely human and familiar from earlier poets and orators, not divine or unique.
rows.anchor: It was something which existed from previous times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell's horror is beyond worldly imagination, and this general warning is not directed at Muhammad.
rows.anchor: Its horror cannot be imagined in this world. Only those will have an idea of it who encounter it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression means Hell will show no mercy by easing agony and will spare no one; it is wholly ruthless and vigilant.
rows.anchor: to show mercy and clemency.” Though the preposition is not mentioned here and neither is there any occasion for its mention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flames burn criminals' skin from a distance, showing how intense the torment's onset is; 70:16 likewise says it strips the skin.
rows.anchor: the skin of the criminals will start to burn even from a distance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verse identifies the unexpressed noun with nineteen as angels; their appearance and powers suit their duty and leave no prospect of escape.
rows.anchor: the succeeding verse tells us that this number refers to angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The realities of Paradise and Hell are mutashābihāt: similes give a general idea, but their actual form is known only to God; insisting on the form risks rejection of reasoned truths.
rows.anchor: the actual form and reality are only known to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 3:7 teaches that warped readers chase ambiguous passages, while grounded believers accept them as revelation and leave their reality to God.
rows.anchor: no one except God knows their reality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nineteen angels prompt mischief among corrupt Quraysh and People of the Book, so the following warning prepares readers while increasing true students' knowledge.
rows.anchor: Such warped personalities always exist

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is an immediate warning revealed with the preceding one: its opening conjunction links it to that verse, unlike a later, independent insertion.
rows.anchor: connected to the previous verse and revealed together with it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The independent Medinan verse 73:20 illustrates how a later insertion differs from this closely connected verse.
rows.anchor: It does not begin with a copulative particle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told that mockery is expected, but he must ignore the arrogant talk; God mentions these facts to strengthen believers and expose mischief-makers.
rows.anchor: must not pay any attention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God appoints angels rather than jinn or devils over Hell, just as angels manage the universe's affairs as pure servants who carry out His will without deviation.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has appointed angels and not the jinn and devils to conduct all the affairs of this universe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that angels are also in Hell is answered by distinguishing prison inmates from their guards; the condemned will learn the difference.
rows.anchor: they should remember that there is a world of difference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nineteen are a trial exposing hidden vice in wrongdoers and virtue in the righteous; tests reveal character and potential.
rows.anchor: hidden vices of the wrong-doers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's heavenly journey and the Qur'an's mention of Hell's zaqqūm tree are other facts that opponents turned into trials and mocked.
rows.anchor: a trial for the opponents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives devils an opportunity to oppose truth so the diseased and hardened are tested and knowledgeable people recognize truth; Islahi refers readers to his discussion of 22:53–54.
rows.anchor: God gives this chance so that what the devils say against the truth becomes a trial

rows.speaker: narratives
rows.claim: Some reports say arrogant Quraysh mocked that nineteen angels were easy to overpower, with one man boasting he and a companion could handle them.
rows.anchor: some narratives that when

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām expresses consequence: the trial increases the certainty of sincere People of the Book and strengthens believers' faith.
rows.anchor: the consequence of the struggle between good and evil is that the conviction of the true People of the Book will be augmented

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sincere People of the Book had no reason to mock the report because similar descriptions appear in their own books; such people later embraced Islam.
rows.anchor: similar statements were found in their own books

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents' weak objections let believers assess both sides, making their faith reasoned and secure rather than blind and easily shaken.
rows.anchor: He accepts it with full conviction and every trial increases his faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negative clause says trials protect sincere People of the Book and believers from doubt, complementing the preceding positive claim.
rows.anchor: become secure from the onslaughts of doubt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some infer a Medinan date from the mention of People of the Book, Islahi rejects that view: sincere People of the Book were counted among Muslims from the beginning.
rows.anchor: in my opinion this view is not correct

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sincere People of the Book are named with believers from the start to establish their status and role alongside the new Prophet and prepare them for coming trials.
rows.anchor: what role they were required to play

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about people with a disease in their hearts concerns jealous Jews, not hypocrites; Qur'an uses disease for envy as well, directed here at the Ishmaelites and Muhammad.
rows.anchor: this word also refers to jealousy and envy, and on such occasions it refers to the Jews

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jealous Jews and Quraysh disbelievers, unlike sincere People of the Book, share a mocking response to ambiguous passages, asking what God means by them.
rows.anchor: the jealous Jews are mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's leading astray or guiding through such trials follows His wise law: He misguides those who merit it and guides those worthy under that law.
rows.anchor: He leads only those people astray whom He finds worthy of this treatment and those who are worthy of being guided as per His law are guided by Him
